Gujarat within the Indian classical music tradition

Gujarat has an important place within the wider Hindustani classical music tradition. Its contribution includes historical musical centres, devotional compositions, distinguished musicians, royal patronage and institutions for formal musical education.

Tana and Riri of Vadnagar

Tana and Riri are celebrated figures in Gujarat's musical heritage. They are traditionally remembered as 2 gifted sisters associated with Vadnagar in Mehsana district.

According to a well-known musical legend, Tansen experienced intense suffering after singing Raga Deepak. Tana and Riri relieved his suffering by singing Malhar, a raga associated with the rainy season.

The story illustrates Gujarat's traditional association with Hindustani ragas and its recognition of accomplished women musicians. The miraculous elements of the account belong to folklore rather than verified physical effects of music.

The sisters are commemorated through a memorial at Vadnagar and the Tana Riri Mahotsav, a musical festival dedicated to their legacy.

Tana and Riri are associated with Vadnagar, Mehsana district, and the traditional musical narrative involving Tansen, Raga Deepak and Malhar.

Baroda as a centre of musical education

The princely state of Baroda became an important centre for the patronage and institutional development of Indian classical music under Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III.

In 1886, a music school known as the Gayan Shala was established in Baroda under his patronage. Ustad Mawla Bux, also spelled Maula Bakhsh, was its founding principal and played an important role in formal musical education.

The institution subsequently developed into the educational tradition represented by the Faculty of Performing Arts of the Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Vadodara.

Royal patronage supported musicians from different musical lineages and helped create an environment for the study and transmission of classical music beyond hereditary musical families.

Devotional music and regional traditions

Narsinh Mehta

Narsinh Mehta was a 15th-century Gujarati devotional poet associated particularly with Junagadh. His musical and literary heritage includes devotional padas, bhajans and Prabhatiyas.

The bhajan Vaishnav Jan To is traditionally attributed to him and is among the best-known works associated with Gujarat's devotional tradition.

Haveli Sangeet

Haveli Sangeet is a devotional musical tradition associated with the Pushtimarg Vaishnava tradition, particularly in Gujarat and Rajasthan. It uses musical compositions and ragas as part of devotional worship.

Although devotional and classical musical traditions interact, a devotional tradition such as Haveli Sangeet should not automatically be classified as a separate system of Indian classical music alongside Hindustani and Carnatic music.

Consolidated revision

The basic framework of Indian classical music consists of swara, raga and tala. Its 2 principal systems are Hindustani and Carnatic music. Hindustani music is associated with forms such as Dhrupad, Khayal and Tarana, while Carnatic music includes Kriti, Varnam and Tillana.

The major chronological sequence is Amir Khusro, Tansen and Tyagaraja. Tyagaraja belongs to the Carnatic Trinity together with Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri. Gujarat's important classical music associations include Tana and Riri of Vadnagar and the Gayan Shala established in Baroda in 1886.

Prelims focus

  • Tana and Riri: Vadnagar, Mehsana district.
  • Gayan Shala: Baroda, established in 1886 under Sayajirao Gaekwad III.
  • Mawla Bux was the founding principal of Gayan Shala.
  • Faiyaz Khan: Agra gharana; Omkarnath Thakur: Gwalior gharana.
  • Haveli Sangeet is associated with the Pushtimarg devotional tradition.
  • Trap: Tana and Riri are not members of the Carnatic Trinity.
